I may be downvoted to hell for this, but there are benefits to eating organic versions of healthy food (read: *not* organic food, period, but organic versions of already established healthy foods). A lot of the pesticides, herbicides, and radiation treatment that lots of produce get are often considered potential (*small*, but still potential) cancer risks. Plus, with all the controversy around pesticides and the increasing strength of the pests they're intended to ward off, having produce that doesn't use them is a means of attempting to relieve this.

But more important than organic produce is organic animal products. With such huge instances of animal rights abuse in factory farms, where "organic" guarantees at least a certain degree of care and good treatment of the animals, one can see why it may have such wide appeal. Plus, it makes you think differently of the food you're eating when the animal it comes from has differences in the growth hormones it's given, and the health of the animal before it's killed. Plus, it's just more ethical for the animals. Look, obviously in the best case scenario we'd all be vegetarians, and regardless of the situation the animals are still killed for our food. But hey, if you're going to eat meat, wouldn't you rather the animal have lived a more pleasant life rather than suffer in a factory farm with terrible conditions?

So yeah, it's not completely confirmed that organic food is not in any way, shape, or form healthier than conventional food. It also goes way beyond health reasons why people would switch to organic.

QUICKEDIT: It is not confirmed that organic food is not healthier. It is, however, unconfirmed how big of the difference is and that's what skeptics go on about.

We had a huge hype train, and then in the weeks soon after there was a huge hate train. This is something that you need to understand--**it goes both ways**.

For me, I saw it opening night. I absolutely loved it. I then saw it three days later with my family. Still absolutely loved it. Most friends of mine saw it around that same opening week. We all still love it. Some of my friends didn't like it as much--that's fine.

When the hate train started rolling around on the internet, I admit I started to doubt my opinions on the movie. But then I rewatched earlier episodes with a friend (his first time seeing them), and rewatching them, I noticed that while people claim the latest installment is derivative, the feel, and many of its features on a much deeper level, are far different, but they still feel very much like the franchise. Looking back at the latest installment, I was even more fond of it.

After seeing some **people on the internet claim, "the previous films were better than this! At least they were original!"**, I had to go back and watch one of those earlier films (since I do own it) with my brother out of curiosity. We said before watching, "Maybe those earlier films are not actually that bad. Maybe the originals just set a high standard." We were wrong. **And holy shit are those people overreacting**. The latest installment probably should've been another 2 or 3 minutes longer to get some more exposition, but I vastly preferred that to the earlier film, which had at least a solid hour's worth of content I just wished I hadn't seen. **Better to keep me wanting more than wanting enormously less.**

**Over a month afterwards, and I still love the latest installment.** Now that the hate train has mostly rolled by and has settled, I'm even more sure of how much I love the movie. Most of my friends who saw it when it opened loved it. Most of my friends who have just seen it recently loved it. It certainly has flaws, and I want the next installments to be more divergent (which the director claims was the intended effect--that this film would reground and the next ones would take things further), but what I'm most impressed by is that **it was all of the new elements of the film that I loved most** (the new characters, the fact that the antagonist wasn't just a copy of a previous character, humanizing the soldiers, making them actually capable fighters, the overall main new plot, the new action choreography, and the general quality of the filmmaking).

So yeah. I'll claim that the latest installment was really that good. I can't rank it against the earlier films yet because the new trilogy is not complete yet and both trilogies rely on their neighboring movies, but I can easily say that I enjoyed it far more than any of the previous films. A few things:

1) Humor is not the same thing as cheese. You seem to be mixing the two. Cheese in movies is actually more like failed melodrama in nature. Or things like puns for comedy. And the exploitation of cheese can be used for clever humor.

I'll actually use one of your examples to demonstrate my point:

>Character A: Wait, why are you helping me?

>Character B: ...because it's the right thing to do.

If the scene had left off over here, that would have been ridiculously cheesy. That's like the silliest trope ever where someone does something good because of some arbitrary sense of what's "right" and "wrong" without any exposure to it.

>[small pause]

>Character A: ...you need a pilot.

>Character B:...I need a pilot.

This actually diverted potential cheese into clever humor, by subverting a typical trope used, and turning it on its head. Suddenly, Character B isn't just some person who somehow is asserting these arbitrary morals that they don't know--they're a desperate opportunist.

2) Different properties have different thresholds of cheese, and different pieces of dialogue have different levels of it. For example, none of these lines, whether humorous or not, would fit at all in a horror film. But in a space opera, they fit perfectly fine. The reason why I still got disrupted by the cheesiness in one recent film is because it got so cheesy it actually crossed even that franchise's line. Which I honestly wasn't sure was so possible.

3) Delivery is also key. Every single one of the lines you cited could've been too cheesy and stupid in the wrong actor's hands, or with bad direction. But each of those moments you cited were delivered extremely well, with tone to match. So it worked, and never took me out of the film. But with that recent film, half of the time there was a cheesy line it was delivered *extremely* poorly, or given bad direction so the inflection was off. Or, just didn't belong tone-wise. It also hurts the movie because it was supposed to be a grittier title, and yet it was even cheesier than another recent installment, so there was some stark and distracting tonal inconsistency.

EDIT: Alright, fine, I'll indulge all of you who are downvoting.

It is well-documented at this point that this game's physics and chemistry engines are on another level compared to just about every open world game. There's a reason it was number 3 on a prominent gaming analysis outlet's most technically impressive games of the year list.

Context-free world interaction is not easy to pull off, and brushing it off like it's no big deal is foolish.

- That electricity reacts differently in different weather, across different materials, is one thing.
- That fire reacts differently on different surfaces, in different weather conditions, across different enemies, is one thing.
- That everything is climbable and yet there are still rules around it that keep it polished is one thing.
- That explosives blow up immediately in volcanic environments is one thing.
- That you can control body temperature by clothing change, weapon change, or external environment changes is one thing.
- That even desert environments have realistic weather cycles of hot and cold is one thing.
- That arrows react differently to different materials and can be gathered if stuck to your shield is one thing.
- That there's a full physics engine on top of this for even the most unexpected objects (button switches, weights on every object, projectiles, the main character, etc.) is one thing.
- The fact that snowballs accumulate snow on rolling is one thing.
- That arrows can be manipulated by wind, bow type, and angle fired is one thing.

The fact that all of those things happen in a single open world game and I'm not even close to done listing more is another thing entirely.

And if you say that it's not new or groundbreaking for an open world game, I'll ask you to name a single other open world game that did this kind of stuff.
